reference_sql:
WITH both_years AS (
  SELECT customer_id
  FROM orders
  WHERE customer_id IS NOT NULL
    AND order_ts >= TIMESTAMP '2024-01-01 00:00:00'
    AND order_ts < TIMESTAMP '2025-01-01 00:00:00'
  INTERSECT
  SELECT customer_id
  FROM orders
  WHERE customer_id IS NOT NULL
    AND order_ts >= TIMESTAMP '2025-01-01 00:00:00'
    AND order_ts < TIMESTAMP '2026-01-01 00:00:00'
)
SELECT COUNT(*) AS customers
FROM both_years
alternatives: WITH both_years AS (SELECT customer_id FROM orders WHERE customer_id IS NOT NULL AND year(order_ts) = 2024 INTERSECT SELECT customer_id FROM orders WHERE customer_id IS NOT NULL AND year(order_ts) = 2025) SELECT COUNT(customer_id) AS customers FROM both_years

WITH per_customer AS (SELECT customer_id FROM orders WHERE customer_id IS NOT NULL GROUP BY customer_id HAVING COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE year(order_ts) = 2024) > 0 AND COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE year(order_ts) = 2025) > 0) SELECT COUNT(*) AS customers FROM per_customer

other_way.sql: WITH per_customer AS (SELECT customer_id FROM orders WHERE customer_id IS NOT NULL GROUP BY customer_id HAVING COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE year(order_ts) = 2024) > 0 AND COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE year(order_ts) = 2025) > 0) SELECT COUNT(*) AS customers FROM per_customer
other_way.tradeoff: Grouping by customer and keeping those with orders in both years works too, but INTERSECT states the two lists more plainly.
